notes.meaning: The men of Ephraim were proud and angry because Gideon did not call them to the battle from the very start. They felt left out of the glory and the plunder, so they argued with him fiercely. Even after a great victory from God, human pride can quickly stir up trouble among God's people.

Gideon answered them gently by comparing his small clan to their powerful tribe. He said that their cleanup of the enemy was far greater than all his family's work at the start of the battle. A soft and humble answer often turns away bitter anger.

Gideon reminded the men of Ephraim that God had handed Midian's two princes over to them. By giving them the credit and pointing to God's hand, he calmed their wounded pride. His wise words cooled their tempers and preserved peace among the tribes.

Gideon and his three hundred men crossed the Jordan River in hot pursuit of the remaining enemy. Even though they were completely exhausted and hungry, they refused to stop until the mission was complete. Faith in God gives strength to keep going even when we feel weak.

When Gideon reached the town of Succoth, he asked the residents for loaves of bread for his weary troops. Succoth was an Israelite city, and its people should have gladly supported their brothers who were fighting for their shared freedom. Gideon did not demand soldiers, only food to keep his men moving.

The leaders of Succoth refused to share any food, asking mockingly if Gideon had already captured the Midianite kings. They were cowardly and selfish, caring more about their own safety than trusting God. They feared that if Gideon lost, the Midianites would return and punish them for helping.

Gideon told the leaders of Succoth that when the Lord gave him victory, he would return and punish them. He warned that he would tear their flesh with sharp desert thorns and briars as a harsh whipping. His firm reply showed complete confidence that God would finish the victory.

Gideon went up to the nearby town of Penuel and asked them for bread just as he had asked Succoth. The men of Penuel gave him the exact same cold and mocking refusal. They were fellow Israelites who refused to help God's army in its moment of need.

Gideon warned the people of Penuel that when he returned in peace, he would tear down their strong tower. They trusted in their tall fortress to keep them safe rather than trusting in God. Gideon was certain that the Lord would bring him back safely as a conqueror.

The two Midianite kings were resting at Karkor with the fifteen thousand soldiers left in their army. An enormous force of one hundred and twenty thousand enemy fighters had already been killed. The Midianites thought they were far enough away to be completely safe from pursuit.

Gideon did not take the main highway, but traveled along a desert tent route to catch the enemy off guard. Because the Midianite camp felt safe and relaxed, Gideon was able to launch a surprise attack. God helped this small band of weary men strike a much larger force.

When the attack began, panic swept through the camp and the two Midianite kings ran for their lives. Gideon chased them down, captured both kings, and scattered their entire army. God completely finished the deliverance He had promised to Israel.

Gideon headed back from the battle along the mountain path called the Ascent of Heres. This route brought him straight toward the cities that had insulted him earlier. He was now ready to hold accountable the fellow Israelites who had refused to help his army.

Just outside Succoth, Gideon caught a young man from the town and questioned him. The youth wrote down a list of seventy-seven city leaders and elders who held authority there. This allowed Gideon to punish the guilty officials without harming the ordinary citizens.

Gideon entered Succoth and presented the captured Midianite kings to the rulers who had mocked him. He repeated the exact words they had used when they refused bread to his exhausted men. Their proud doubts were proved wrong by the clear evidence of God's victory.

Gideon gathered the elders of Succoth and punished them by beating them with desert thorns and briars. This painful discipline taught the leaders that betraying God's servants and mocking His work brings severe judgment. It served as a stern warning to all the people of the city.

Gideon then went to Penuel, broke down their fortified tower, and killed the men of that city. The people of Penuel had placed their confidence in stone walls while defying the Lord's chosen deliverer. Their proud rebellion led to their complete destruction.

Gideon questioned the two Midianite kings about the men they had murdered earlier at Mount Tabor. The kings admitted the killings and said the victims looked majestic, just like Gideon himself. Gideon recognized from their description that the slain men were his own family members.

Gideon declared that the murdered men were his full brothers, the sons of his own mother. He swore by the living Lord that he would have spared the kings' lives if they had not killed his brothers. As the nearest relative, Gideon had the duty under ancient law to avenge the murder of his family.

Gideon told his oldest son, Jether, to draw his sword and execute the captive kings. He wanted to honor his son and teach him courage against Israel's enemies. The boy was too young and afraid, so he could not bring himself to draw his sword.

The captive kings urged Gideon to strike them down himself, knowing a mighty warrior would kill them quickly and with less shame. Gideon stepped forward, executed them, and took the golden crescent ornaments from their camels. Evil rulers will always face God's justice in the end.

The people of Israel asked Gideon to rule over them as king and to establish a family dynasty of rulers. They were grateful for the great rescue from Midian and wanted a permanent human leader to protect them. In their excitement, they began looking to a man rather than trusting God as their true King.

Gideon firmly refused the crown, saying neither he nor his son would rule over Israel. He told them that the Lord alone was their true King and ruler. This humble answer honored God and put the focus back where it belonged.

Although Gideon turned down the crown, he asked the Israelites for a gift of gold earrings taken from the battle plunder. The Midianites and other eastern desert tribes were known for wearing heavy gold jewelry. Gideon asked for this wealth even after making a noble spiritual statement.

The people gladly agreed to his request and spread out a large cloak on the ground. Each man eagerly tossed a gold ring from his share of the spoils onto the garment. Their willing generosity showed their great admiration for Gideon, even though the result would soon turn dangerous.

The weight of the gold rings came to about forty to fifty pounds, a massive fortune. Gideon also received golden crescent pendants, fine purple royal robes, and ornamental chains taken from the camels. The huge pile of treasure showed the complete defeat of the Midianite army.

Gideon used some of the gold to make an ephod, a special priestly garment, and set it up in his hometown of Ophrah. Although Gideon may have wanted to remember God's victory, the people began worshiping it as an idol. This unlawful shrine led Israel into sin and brought trouble upon Gideon's own family.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars think Gideon's ephod was a gold-plated image or idol rather than just a priestly garment.

notes.meaning: Midian was so thoroughly crushed that it never posed a threat to Israel again. The land enjoyed peace and security for forty years throughout Gideon's lifetime. God remained faithful to give His people rest whenever they turned to Him for rescue.

Gideon, also known as Jerubbaal, returned to his hometown and lived in his own house. With the war over, he stepped back from the battlefield to lead the nation as a judge. He chose to live in his family estate rather than building a royal court like a king.

Gideon had seventy sons because he took many wives. While large families were seen as a blessing, having a harem of wives imitated the pagan kings around him and broke God's ideal for marriage. This accumulation of wives set the stage for bitter conflict among his children later on.

Gideon also had a concubine, a secondary wife, living in the city of Shechem, who gave birth to a son named Abimelech. The name Abimelech means 'my father is king.' Even though Gideon had refused the title of king, this name revealed an unhealthy royal ambition that would bring future disaster.

Gideon lived a long life, died at a good old age, and was buried in his father's family tomb in Ophrah. A long, peaceful life was recognized in Israel as a sign of God's favor. Yet the compromises he made in his later years left behind dangerous seeds for the next generation.

As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites turned away from God and went back to worshiping the Canaanite Baals. They made a special covenant with an idol called Baal-berith, meaning 'lord of the covenant.' Without godly leadership, the people quickly fell into spiritual unfaithfulness.

The people of Israel forgot the Lord their God who had rescued them from all the surrounding enemies. Their quick return to idolatry showed deep ingratitude for all the wonders God had done in their history. Forgetting God's past goodness makes it easy to slip into sin.

The Israelites also failed to show loyalty or kindness to Gideon's family, despite everything he had done to save them from Midian. People who forget their duty to God usually forget their duty to their fellow human beings as well. Human praise is fickle and soon fades once a great leader is gone.
